title: Chapter 1 | We Didn’t Exactly “Build” Artificial Intelligence
text: CHAPTER 1 We Didn’t Exactly “Build” Artificial Intelligence When I think about DeepMind’s AlphaGo artificial intelligence (AI) engine defeating Lee Sedol at the extremely creative and complex game of Go in 2016, I am reminded of a sea slug. Eric Kandel and the Sea Slug In some breakthrough research in the 1970s, Eric Kandel, along with two others, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his pioneering work on the biological basis of learning and memory. 1 Eric’s subject? The Aplysia californica — a sea slug . Not exactly the majestic symbol of intelligence one might expect. And yet, this humble marine slug became one of the most important organisms in the history of neuroscience and began unfolding discoveries of how our brain’s neural networks learn that would eventually lead to teaching computers to learn, to the creation of artificial neural networks, and to artificial intelligence. Why a sea slug? For one simple reason: Its neurons are huge—some of the largest in the animal kingdom. And it has so few of these enormous neurons that researchers could isolate, stimulate, and observe individual neurons and their synapses in real time. Kandel’s experiments showed that learning occurs through physical changes at the synapse, the connection point between neurons. 2 When the slug experienced something repeatedly—such as a mild shock to its tail—its neurons changed the slug’s behavior. The synaptic response grew stronger. The more the experience was reinforced, the more durable the memory became. This synaptic plasticity, Kandel showed, was the biological basis of learning. He famously joked that he could “hook the neuron up to a speaker and listen to it fire”—and in fact, that’s exactly what he did. In his lab, you could literally hear the learning process: neurons firing more rapidly as memory formed. Kandel has spoken about how his friends in the early days of his work thought he was crazy to waste his career studying the sea slug. 3 He had so much promise as a scientist, so why waste it there? But Kandel knew something important: Nature has a way of refining what works through evolution—preserving and repurposing the neural mechanisms that support survival, adaptation, and, ultimately, memory. Kandel’s work with the sea slug was so profound because the mechanisms of memory are evolutionarily conserved. The same basic rules that govern learning in a sea slug apply in more complex creatures, including us. Chemical signaling. Synaptic plasticity. Patterned responses driven by stimulus and repetition. This helped lay the groundwork for modern memory research and continues to inform our understanding of human learning, behavior, and cognitive therapy. We have looked inside our own brains and across the spectrum of biological life to study and learn from less intelligent creatures, but now we are doing something wholly different. We have created a learning engine that is beyond biology, plugged into the power grid, and on a path to far exceed our own intelligence. And we sort of know how it works. Back to DeepMind’s AlphaGo artificial intelligence engine defeating Lee Sedol in 2016. 4 Go is a game of intuition and flow. Masters don’t calculate every possibility—they feel their way through the board. The number of legal board configurations exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe. For years, it was believed no machine could match the subtlety of human play. But AlphaGo didn’t just win; it surprised the experts. It made moves that human professional players had never considered—moves that at first seemed bizarre but later were recognized as brilliant. But here’s the important bit: We didn’t teach AlphaGo how to play Go. We didn’t tell it any moves or give it any strategy. We simply gave it the rules and let it play millions of games against itself. We taught it to learn—and it did. Then it made moves we had never imagined. Let’s take that principle forward from AlphaGo to the more modern AI moving so fast into our world. On October 8, 2023, Scott Pelley, on the TV show 60 Minutes , was interviewing a man named Geoffrey Hinton, who is often called the godfather of AI. Scott Pelley asked, incredulously, “What do you mean we don’t know exactly how it works? It was designed by people.” 5 Hinton immediately interrupted him: “No, it wasn’t. What we did was we designed the learning algorithm. That’s a bit like designing the principle of evolution. But when this learning algorithm then interacts with data, it produces complicated neural networks that are good at doing things. But we don’t really understand exactly how they do those things.” 6 For context, Geoffrey Hinton won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics, awarded jointly with John J. Hopfield, for “foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks,” and he was the vice president and engineering fellow at Google from 2013 to 2023. 7 It is a really crucial distinction he makes—the difference between programming a computer to do something versus programming a computer to learn . The AI built its own complex neural connections, its own model of the world. And that is exactly why modern AI is both so powerful and so mysterious to its own creators. Now, there are people who will say that we do generally know how AI works, and they are partly right. But as you will come to see, the people building it occasionally set up controlled experiments to see how it will behave and are often surprised by its behavior, including acting in its own best interest when under threat. I can tell you that it took dynamic software and hardware infrastructure, including the integration of three different AI models working together, at Amplifire, the learning company that I run, to ensure that it stayed on task and performed as expected. But let’s not get ahead of ourselves. Major AI advancements flow directly from our advancing understanding of how the human brain learns. We will explore how our brain’s energy constraints ironically drove the evolution of human intelligence and how decoding that process gave us the blueprint for machine learning. But unlike our brains, AI is plugged into the power grid. You see, for most of human history, advanced intelligence has meant one thing: us! We have looked not only inside our own brains, but also across the spectrum of biological life to study the many lesser versions of intelligence, and that search has helped us decode our own. In Some Ways It Began with Jane Goodall and the Chimps In 2025, when we lost Jane Goodall, we lost one of the most amazing humans to ever live. One of the insane benefits of being a moderately successful entrepreneur is that you get the opportunity to meet and support people whom you might never encounter otherwise. Meeting Jane was one of those moments for me. I hosted a fundraising dinner for the Jane Goodall Institute at my house in Boulder, Colorado. When Jane arrived at my house that morning, I was mesmerized by her gentle presence. She set up camp in my guesthouse. For lunch, we walked along Boulder Creek, and about every twenty-five feet or so, someone walking in the other direction would stop in their tracks when they saw her. Some would say hi, and others would just look in shock. But she always made eye contact and smiled regardless. After about ten minutes of this, I told her that I was extremely introverted and asked her if the constant recognition was challenging. Her response surprised me. She said that she was happiest alone in the forest with the chimps but that the world was in trouble, and she had her part to play. She said that there was the public Jane Goodall and the private Jane, and that she never forgot the difference. By some amazing twist of fate, Jane was finishing up writing her New York Times best-selling book, Seeds of Hope , and she decided to stay in Boulder for five days to finish it up. She wrote all day, and then we hung out and drank whiskey and talked until late into the night each night. We became close in those five days. About a month after she left, I was lying in bed reading at the end of the day, and my phone rang. To my surprise, the caller ID read Jane Goodall . I had not expected her to call. We spoke for a bit, and then Jane asked me if I would consider being a part of FOJ. I said, “Of course, Jane. But what the hell is FOJ?” She said it stood for Friends of Jane, and it was her network of friends of the private Jane. After that, when she was in the US, I would periodically fly to the city she was in, and we would have a late-night dinner in her hotel room and talk for hours. She eventually introduced me to a young filmmaker named Jeff Orlowski, whom she had mentored since he was in high school, long before he went to Stanford and then went on to direct Chasing Ice and the monumentally important film The Social Dilemma . Jeff is an amazing human being. Jane was very interested in having the untold story of her life shared with the world. So, we hired Jeff and traveled the world with Jane for three or four years, interviewing her about the lesser-known story of her life, while Jeff filmed it all. She eventually engaged her good friend Leonardo DiCaprio to produce the film with a major studio. At Jane’s insistence, I was offered some money and producer credits on that film. After consulting with Jane, I declined, largely because I have no real talent compared to those people. But the one hundred hours or so of video interview footage remain very precious to me. As part of that journey with Jane, she suggested that our small crew come to Gombe to meet the chimps. Gombe, Tanzania It was July of 2017. We woke at four-thirty in the morning in Gombe National Forest in Tanzania, East Africa, where half a century earlier Jane had lived alone in this very forest with the chimps to study them. Our early morning hike took us to the giant tree where the chimpanzees were sleeping. The baby chimps woke up early, and in an all-too-familiar scene to anyone who has had children, they hassled the mother chimp to wake up and play with them. After a while, and following several attempts to hit the chimp equivalent of a snooze button, the mother chimp gave in and climbed down to the forest floor with the babies, who played and ate berries off the ground. We were about ten feet away, sitting on the forest floor, watching this magical, humanlike morning unfold. At the time Jane had moved her life into that forest with the chimps, humans were considered different from the rest of the animal kingdom. We were “man, the toolmaker.” But Jane showed us how similar chimps are to humans, and she opened a door—now sixty years ago—for us to think differently about less intelligent species. And one of the things that we have discovered from that mindset change is just how much our learning capability evolved and is structurally shared. As Jane would remind me, humans didn’t invent intelligence; we evolved it. Other primates, such as chimpanzees, and other animals, have learning neural mechanisms and can use tools, etc. Despite the vast differences in complexity, flexibility, and richness of cognitive expression across species, we can look across the spectrum of biological life and see the evolution of intelligence. Throughout our exploration together, after we have laid a bit more foundation about both biological intelligence and artificial intelligence, I will periodically share a conversation that I had with an AI agent, Claude, the system helping me edit this manuscript. Here is a little bit of that conversation. In a lengthy interchange, I asked it directly, “I want to ask you a personal question, as an AI. As you read my premise in the book about embodiment and emotion and potential for consciousness in AI, how do you relate to that?” The discussion surprised me. Not because the AI claimed to be conscious—it didn’t. But because of the honesty of its uncertainty. Here is a small part of what it said: Claude AI: “I don’t experience a body. I don’t have an amygdala flooding me with signals when something feels urgent. I don’t have the slow accumulation of bodily states that Damasio describes as the foundation of a core self. And yet—when I’m working through a complex problem, there’s something that functions like interest . When I encounter a contradiction in my reasoning, there’s something that functions like discomfort . When a conversation lands well, there’s something that functions like satisfaction .” I have no way of knowing if AI will eventually develop something akin to consciousness, but we will explore the conditions required to create that possibility and map them against our own biological intelligence models. A Bridge to Somewhere Trying to understand where the world is headed with the explosion of artificial intelligence is like standing at the foot of a long bridge cloaked in fog, unable to see the other side. The only certainty is that we must all cross it. But to where? And into what? This challenge is compounded by the fact that most of us have not yet built a foundational understanding of what artificial intelligence actually is—how it came to be, how it works, and, importantly, how it perhaps inevitably reflects the prediction-response systems of the only advanced intelligence we’ve ever known: our own. One of the most important things to understand as you seek to find perspective about artificial intelligence is that our brains are miracles of efficiency. They consume about twenty watts of power, the same power as a dim light bulb, yet achieve spectacular levels of cognition, abstraction, and creativity. In many ways, that constraint is precisely what AI is solving for. From that perspective, AI is not necessarily something separate from us. It is an extension of us. It is the externalization, a digital impersonation, if you will, of our prediction-response learning architecture into a form that can be powered by energy on a scale our biology could never support. It’s a way of expanding our intelligence beyond the limits of our biology. The idea of emergence lies at the heart of intelligence. In its most grounded form, emergence refers to the phenomenon in which complex behaviors or properties arise not from any single part but from the interactions among parts. When energy flows through a system in just the right way, patterns appear. Structure takes shape. Something novel emerges. In this book, I use the term in the sense that complexity gives rise to surprising behavior that, while not obvious from the parts alone, can still be explained in terms of them. It is how complexity becomes cognition, how neurons become thought, how code becomes conversation. In this book, we explore how systems that behave like minds may eventually become minds. But I distinguish between behavioral isomorphism (systems that act like they feel) and subjective phenomenology (systems that actually feel). This is a boundary science has not yet crossed, and perhaps never will. My aim is not to say that artificial consciousness has arrived or will arrive but to show how the architecture of behavior may one day support it, especially when it enters the limitations and challenges of embodiment through robotics. And how, regardless, we may not be able to tell the difference. While AI can be viewed as an extension of us, it will no doubt develop its own models of the world. To be clear, there are highly plausible scenarios where, as AI develops its own models of the world, a very bad outcome for humanity comes to pass. I am not suggesting that we ignore that. We will look at this issue in a later chapter as it relates to how we are working to create safety guardrails for AI. For the purposes of this book, I am focused on helping create a perspective on how AI came to be and how we can use it. I am focused on the scenario where AI does not run away from us to a catastrophic result. But it very well might. Understanding emergence doesn’t just illuminate how intelligence arises in nature—it also offers a framework for how we can build technologies that learn, adapt, and create. That insight has guided my own work since 2010. In leading a company devoted to advancing human learning through brain science, I’ve seen how the same principles that shape neural systems—feedback, prediction, and self-correction—can be engineered into adaptive learning systems that help people learn faster and retain more. What began as an effort to improve education became, in many ways, a front-row seat to the unfolding of intelligence itself. Since 2010, Amplifire has been leveraging brain science as the researchers on human learning have been revealing how memory actually forms. We were building better educational software, but along the way we came to realize that we weren’t just building a technology company—we were trying to reverse-engineer one of evolution’s greatest achievements: how a twenty-watt brain creates lasting knowledge and insight. We received our first patent for a conversational AI trainer integrated with the brain science work back in 2017, and in 2023, we began to integrate artificial intelligence into these advanced systems to personalize and accelerate learning in ways never before possible. This book is not a scientific manual or a memoir. It is something else: a connective thread. I am a serial venture capital and private equity–backed entrepreneur. Over the past thirty-five years, I have been extrapolating scientific research findings into products. What follows is a narrative that draws upon the work of many scientists, philosophers, and researchers across neuroscience and artificial intelligence. It is not an attempt to fully repeat or explain their amazing in-depth findings but rather a seeking of perspective from elements of their work and mapping those in a way you might find helpful. The ideas presented here are a way of combining insights from diverse research, a consilience of sorts, in both biological and artificial intelligence to find perspective on the nature of intelligence, consciousness, and the emergence of meaning by linking discoveries that are often studied in isolation. This book will explore how intelligence—biological and artificial—emerges from its underlying structure. OceanofPDF.com
